items.title: Researchers demonstrate Firecracker microVM escape achieving root code execution on host via KVM return frame manipulation
items.originalTitle: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
items.summary:
Researchers detailed a vulnerability in Firecracker microVMs that allowed them to escape the VM and execute code as root on the host. They exploited the saved register state of Firecracker's vCPU threads during KVM_RUN system calls to redirect execution flow upon return to userspace, maintaining VM accessibility over SSH.

The attack involved identifying the Firecracker process and its memory mappings from within the guest by translating guest physical addresses to host physical addresses using Extended Page Tables. By locating the saved register frames and modifying them, the researchers took control of a live thread in the Firecracker process. This work builds on a prior memory primitive exploit and demonstrates CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.

This vulnerability highlights risks in microVM isolation mechanisms and may prompt security reviews and patches in Firecracker deployments to prevent similar escapes and privilege escalations.

items.title: New York Times sues Brave over alleged unauthorized copying and sale of over 30 billion webpages to AI companies including Anthropic and Cohere [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Brave Sells Its Search Index to AI, and Your Website Is Probably in It
items.summary:
The New York Times has filed a lawsuit against Brave, accusing the company of copying more than 30 billion webpages without identifying its crawler or providing website owners a way to block it, then selling this content to AI firms through its Brave Search API. Brave's crawler does not use a unique user agent, making it impossible for websites to block Brave without also blocking Google, as Brave follows Google's crawling rules. Brave sells access to its index to AI companies such as Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and others, enabling AI assistants to retrieve recent web content without directly scraping the web themselves.

The lawsuit also highlights that Brave's index provides AI companies with extracted page content and metadata formatted for large language models, which may be used to generate answers without directing users back to the original websites. Brave has not yet responded to the lawsuit, and the case raises questions about the legality and ethics of selling web indexes to AI companies without website owners' consent or control over how their content is used.

items.originalTitle: YC Backed Bron AI Accused of Using LeBron's Name and Likeness
items.summary:
LeBron James has issued a cease and desist letter to Bron AI, a Y Combinator-backed startup, for using his name, likeness, and persona without permission in an AI-powered sports betting app. The app's promotional video featured a character resembling James, wearing his jersey number and nickname, implying an association that James denies and which violates NBA rules due to his exclusive endorsement deal with Polymarket.

The letter demands Bron AI remove the ad and notify users that James is not involved with the company. The ad also included images of other athletes like Donovan Mitchell and Luka Dončić, who has also sent a cease and desist. Legal experts called the ad a clear infringement on publicity rights, and the incident has raised questions about due diligence and intellectual property use in sports marketing and AI applications.

items.title: DeepMind AI agents identify two vulnerabilities in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems, reducing computational effort needed to compromise them [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeepMind AI agents find two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems
items.summary:
DeepMind researchers have used AI agents to uncover two significant weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems, demonstrating that these systems can be compromised with less computational power than previously believed. Their findings focus on digital signature forgery when attackers control half or more of the signed block and a new algorithm that improves factorization efficiency for keys of the same size.

The research shows that padding in digital signatures offers no protection if an attacker controls roughly half the block, enabling forgery with significantly reduced CPU time. Additionally, the AI agents discovered an algorithm that lowers the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times compared to prior batch methods. These results apply to obsolete 1024-bit RSA systems, while modern protocols using 2048-bit or larger keys remain secure.

This work highlights how AI can accelerate cryptanalysis and challenges the assumption that cryptographic hardness is static, emphasizing the need for ongoing stress-testing to maintain the security of modern encryption standards.

Apple earlier this year hiked prices for its devices, citing rising memory costs.

items.originalTitle: Chesky’s Side Quest
items.summary:
Once upon a time, being CEO of a public company was a full-time job. In fact, for most CEOs, it still is—and an exhausting one at that. So it’s a little puzzling to see that a growing number of tech CEOs are embarking on their own side quests, including most recently Airbnb’s Brian Chesky, who has started an AI lab, as Bloomberg reported earlier this year.

Airbnb disclosed Thursday, as it reported third-quarter earnings, that it had sold some intellectual property to Chesky’s new venture for $7.1 million in cash. Airbnb also got the right to invest in any future equity financings of the venture and to license “certain” IP of the lab for internal use in Airbnb’s business. (Hopefully, the IP Airbnb will license isn’t the same IP it just sold to the lab.) Get this: It’s not just Chesky who is involved. Airbnb Chief Technology Officer Ahmad Al-Dahle also has equity in the venture and, like Chesky, “performs services” for it.

items.title: Can Cheaper AI Outrun the Data Center Backlash? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Cheaper AI Outrun the Data Center Backlash?
items.summary:
After U.S. voters on Tuesday elected officials who are pushing to restrict data center expansion, some tech executives and investors are concerned that new delays in standing up computing capacity will make existing servers for AI more expensive to run.

And if computing becomes even pricier, there’s a question of whether declines in the cost of running AI could slow down.

So far this year, the cost of running AI has been falling, even as the price of renting servers has risen. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, released in late September, can perform comparably to a bigger OpenAI flagship model, GPT-6 Astra, when used with a high reasoning setting. Yet the newer model costs about a fifth as much on a per-task basis as the older model, research firm Artificial Analysis said.

Anthropic has touted similar efficiencies with its latest models. And that’s happening despite the fact that buying or renting Nvidia hardware has gotten a lot costlier this year.

As AI costs become a major concern at enterprises, the price-drop trend will need to persist or else customers might pull back.

One senior executive of a private equity firm that owns and develops data centers told me this week that they believe prices of AI models will keep falling due to “token efficiencies”—the ability of AI to do more work with less compute—thanks to both hardware and software advancements.

In other words, they said, such efficiencies would help offset constraints on data center expansion. Of course, the executive is heavily incentivized to say such things, given the financial bets their company has already made.

On Wednesday, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said during an event hosted by private equity firm Blackstone that he is optimistic about the company’s data center expansion despite the election results. “We feel like we're in a pretty good spot, and I think others may have some more work to do.”

To be sure, Amazon has faced significant local resistance to some of its data center projects, and even had to drop a project in Virginia this year.

Garman didn’t comment on whether he expects server rental prices to rise further. But stock investors seemed to think so initially, based on the way they bid up shares of major cloud providers Wednesday while selling off stocks of smaller cloud providers that still need approvals for new facilities. (The major cloud providers pared back some of the gains during a selloff Thursday.)

Notably, many facilities that are supposed to come online next year have gotten some or all of the necessary state or local approvals, so the effects of the electoral backlash might have a big impact on facilities aiming to launch in 2028 and beyond.

Anthropic’s initial public offering prospectus offers another signal that the price of using its models has room to fall: the company’s gross profit margins have hovered around 85% in the first nine months of the year. (That excludes the cost of developing the models themselves.) So it may have some slack to lower prices if it needs to boost demand.
